extracted.intended_audience: health researchers (authors) writing manuscripts; journal editors and reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on what information to include when reporting health research so manuscripts are transparent, reproducible, and usable for clinical and evidence-synthesis purposes. Covers the nature, format, and development standards of reporting guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — ensure manuscript can be understood by a reader
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline provides a minimum list of information needed to ensure a manuscript can be understood by a reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting guidelines are intended to help authors include the essential information so readers can follow the study rationale, methods, results, and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — ensure manuscript can be replicated by a researcher
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline provides a minimum list of information needed to ensure a manuscript can be replicated by a researcher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes sufficient methodological detail and data reporting to allow independent researchers to reproduce the study or repeat analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — ensure manuscript can be used by a clinician to make decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline provides a minimum list of information needed to ensure a manuscript can be used by a doctor to make a clinical decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises clear reporting of clinical applicability, interventions, outcomes, harms, and relevant contexts so clinicians can judge relevance to patient care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — ensure manuscript can be included in a systematic review
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporting guideline provides a minimum list of information needed to ensure a manuscript can be included in a systematic review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitates identification, appraisal, and data extraction by systematic reviewers by standardising key items and reporting formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — checklist/flow diagram/structured text developed using explicit methodology
rubrics_metrics.description: “A checklist, flow diagram, or structured text to guide authors in reporting a specific type of research, developed using explicit methodology.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting guidelines are formal tools (not informal notes) and must be developed through an explicit, documented methodology rather than ad hoc opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation — must present a clear list of reporting items
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether presented as structured text or a checklist, a reporting guideline presents a clear list of reporting items that should appear in a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines should organise and present required items clearly so authors can systematically check items when preparing a manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development transparency — must explain how the list was developed
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether presented as structured text or a checklist, a reporting guideline explains how the list was developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good guidelines document their development process (e.g., consensus methods, literature review, stakeholder involvement) so users can assess credibility and scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability — specific guidelines exist for main study types
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting guidelines exist for key study types (randomised trials, observational studies, systematic reviews, study protocols, diagnostic/prognostic studies, case reports, clinical practice guidelines, qualitative research, animal pre-clinical studies, quality improvement, economic evaluations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include CONSORT (randomised trials), STROBE (observational), PRISMA (systematic reviews), SPIRIT/PRISMA-P (protocols), STARD/TRIPOD (diagnostic/prognostic), CARE (case reports), AGREE/RIGHT (clinical practice guidelines), SRQR/COREQ (qualitative), ARRIVE (animal studies), SQUIRE (quality improvement), CHEERS (economic evaluations). Extensions may exist for specific designs or interventions.
